tigers gamer 0712

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

MINNEAPOLIS -- Momentum, Brad Ausmus and many other baseball men have said, is the next day's starting pitcher. 
"It certainly makes a big difference," he said.
And with Friday night's ninth inning fiasco in the rearview mirror -- the back-end of the Tigers bullpen blew a five-run lead in the ninth inning, beat on Brian Dozier's three-run, walk-off home run -- the Twins seemingly had all the momentum in this four-game series.
And with right-hander Alfredo Simon on the hill today, the Tigers certainly did not.
Simon was roughed up once again, allowing seven runs -- five earned -- on 10 hits as the Tigers were railed by the Twins, 9-5, at Target Field.
"All my pitches were up and I was behind in the count," Simon said. 
For the fifth consecutive start, Simon allowed five or more earned runs. He was hit early and he was hit often and he was hit hard.
"It's been a bad stretch for him, for sure," Ausmus said. "Obviously we need to get him past that sooner rather than later."
In the second inning, he allowed five consecutive hits to open the inning. In the third inning, he allowed four consecutive hits before getting chased.
Simon's line looked like this: 2 2/3 innings pitched, seven runs, five earned runs, no walks, one strikeout.
Asked if the team will consider removing him from the starting rotation, Ausmus said: "We aren't right now."
Once again, he dug the Tigers too deep a hole to climb out of, although they tried. They responded with three runs in the third inning -- Victor Martinez hit his fifth home run, a solo shot to rightfield and James McCann singled home two runs -- but after former Tiger Torii Hunter hit a two-run home run in the sixth inning off righty Buck Farmer, they were toast, and will have to win on Sunday to salvage a series split.
"We were chipping away then to tack on two runs," Ausmus said, "That kind of stings."
Farmer relieved Simon and threw 3 1/3 solid innings, allowing two runs on five hits. He struck out four and walked one. 
But their offense went silent after that lone run in the fifth inning, courtesy of a Yoenis Cespedes ground-rule double, right after Martinez spoke his mind to home plate umpire Marty Foster after a questionable called third strike.
"I haven't seen him get that angry with a call," Ausmus said.
The Tigers tacked on a run in the seventh inning, but it was too little, too late.
Right-handed reliever Neftali Feliz, signed earlier today, made his team debut in the eighth inning. He allowed  an infield hit and struck out one.
After Simon was smacked around, the Tigers trail the Royals by eight games in the American League Central. 
"Yeah, I think so," he said, when asked if he was in the midst of the most frustrating stretch of pitching in his career. "I just have to pitch better in the second half."
The first half ends on Sunday.
"We need to win and split the series," Ausmus said.
If they don't, they will continue to split away from the pack.
tigers six 0712

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

Shane Greene was waiting for it to click. 
And when he struggled through a second consecutive month heading into the middle of June, instead of thinking about getting big-league hitters out, he was searching for it to click.
After getting optioned to Triple-A Toledo on June 12, he said on Saturday morning at Target Field, "I didn't have to worry about getting them out as much as try to find myself on the mound."
Greene, who will start the first half finale on Sunday against the Twins, thinks he found himself on the mound in his five starts with the Mud Hens.
He posted a 3.42 ERA, allowing 10 runs on 29 hits in 26 1/3 innings. He struck out 14.
But most importantly, the Tigers right-hander said, he found his slider.
"That's the pitch that got me to the big leagues and I haven't had it since spring training," Greene said.
He carried the mechanical changes he started to make in Detroit with him to Toledo -- speeding up his arm and keeping his weight on his back side -- and, "I started to feel a lot better," he said. "I don't have to think about it as much now. It's second nature. I'm pretty happy with everything."
Greene started the season strong but faded fast, posting a 5.82 ERA in 13 starts with the Tigers.
Manager Brad Ausmus has not said who will be the team's fifth starter after the All-Star break.
"It was no secret that I was struggling," Greene said. "Something needed to happen. It was a lot easier where the spotlight was not as big.
Along with his slider, he said his change up has come along.
"I feel good," he said. "I just want to keep building off it."
tigers notes 0713

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

MINNEAPOLIS -- Dave Dombrowski doesn't have an All-Star break.
"You're not going anywhere," he said.
And a day before the Tigers take a four-day vacation, Dombrowski sat down with reporters and spoke about the first half, talking about the current state of the team ad their immediate future with the trade deadline looming.
"Not particularly pleased with where we are," he said. "But we're also in a position where if we play up to our capabilities in the second half, we have a chance to win still."
The Tigers are 44-43. They trail the Royals by eight games in the American League Central and stand 1 1/2 games behind the second Wild Card spot in the AL.
"We have been very inconsistent through the first half," Dombrowski said. "We haven't really been on a roll since the beginning of the season."
And that, he said, is the most surprising thing about the season so far.
But ranking close behind is the pitching staff, both the starting rotation and bullpen, which has underperformed.
“Probably I am a little surprised our pitching hasn’t been better overall, as a whole," he said. "When I say that you have to be careful because some guys have pitched very well. But overall as a group, I am surprised we haven’t pitched a little better."
The Tigers rank XXXXXth in the AL in ERA. Their starters, XXXXXth and their bullpen, XXXXXth.
“People point to bullpen, but a lot of times your bullpen can be exposed if the starters aren’t going well," he said. "And we’re in a stretch where our starters haven’t given us a lot of innings.”
Right-handers Shane Greene and Alfredo Simon started off strong, but Greene spent a month in Triple-A and Simon has allowed five or more runs in five consecutive games.
And with an improved as of late offense, the pitching staff stands out in the team's trade deadline needs, although Dombrowski wouldn't speculate on such moves.
"We'll see," he said.
Dombrowski stressed that the Tigers, "We're trying to win right now," and that, "There have been many clubs that have been eight games behind -- more than that -- at this time of the year and have made those games up. We have a club that has some ability."
The Tigers would rather not be this far back in the standings, he said, "But again, we haven't gotten on a streak and there's no reason to say we can't."
He didn't delve deeply into the team's impending superstar free agents like starting pitcher David Price and leftfielder Yoenis Cespedes but did say that the team hoped to sign Price, one of the best left-handed starters in the game, long-term.
Assessing manager Brad Ausmus this season, Dombrowski said, "Brad's done fine. I think we're all in a situation where for us, none of us are pleased with where we are and I can say that, including Brad. Brad has done a fine job."
In years past, Dombrowski has made moves in July to beef up the team's talent for a postseason run and this year appears to be no different with the team still within a streak of cutting into the Royals' lead and striking distance of a Wild Card berth.
"I don't think it impacts it much," he said when asked how the division and Wild Card races could affect their aggressiveness going forward. "I think you're trying to win your division, that's what your goal is. If that doesn't happen then you do the best job you can (to win the Wild Card) but I don't think it really changes anything. You're definitely trying to win your division."
But if the Tigers don't turn the tide soon, they will find themselves double-digit games behind the top spot in a much tougher AL Central than in years past.
And Dombrowski made it clear that this group of players needs to start righting the ship.
"We have to get on a roll at some point," he said. "We have to. We’re not going to be able to play a couple of games, get three games above, then one game above. ... We're going to have to start playing better, we're just going to have to."
tigers six 0713

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

MINNEAPOLIS -- Dave Dombrowski is a free agent at the end of the year.
And when the Tigers president and general manager met with reporters before Sunday's series finale against the Twins at Target Field, he said any so-called challenges he might face in navigating a crucial trade deadline is just that: So-called.
"My job every day, no matter how I've been throughout my career -- long-term, short-term, I always approach it the same way," he said. "I always wok as hard as I can and do everything I possibly can."
Dombrowski, 58, has held his current positions since 2002. He signed a four-year extension in Aug. 2011 and would not elaborate on if there was any current progress being made on a new extension.
"I wouldn't get into my own situation," he said.
Dombrowski is the architect of a team that has won four consecutive American League Central championships. Since 2006, the Tigers have reached two World Series  and advanced to the AL Championship Series twice, losing both times. He has one World Series championship to his name, with the Marlins in 1997.
About approaching the trade deadline without a contract next year, Dombrowski said, "We always work as an organization with ownership with whatever their priorities are at a particular time. We always work with the owner in that regard and I've done that my whole career."
tigers gamer 0713

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

MINNEAPOLIS -- It was, they agreed, time for a break.
A break from the bad pitching. A break from the bad fielding. A break from the bad losses -- the baddest of which came on Friday night in fiery fashion, when the Twins burned the back-end of the bullpen for seven runs in the ninth inning -- and a break from baseball.
"I'm going to watch my daughters play softball," Tigers manager Brad Ausmus said half-heartedly. "And not make any lineup decisions or pitching moves."
On Sunday afternoon, no lineup decision or pitching move Ausmus made would matter. Once again, the Tigers tumbled into a tall hole because of a starting pitcher's struggle and they were thwacked by the Twins, 7-1, at Target Field.
This time, it was right-hander Shane Greene, who was making his first start since getting demoted to Triple-A Toledo a month earlier.
Greene allowed seven earned runs on seven hits over 4 2/3 innings and this time, the Tigers offense was unable to mount any sort of a comeback chance.
After being two outs away from taking the first two games of the series on Friday night, the Tigers dropped three of four to the Twins.
"It's simple," Victor Martinez said when asked how to remedy the team's recent woes. "Play better. Be better. Pitch better. Better defense. If any team wants to win, especially a championship, you have to play better. You can't win with the way you're playing right now."
And their downfall was once again the starting pitching.
"I couldn't avoid the big inning and I made two mistakes that I paid for,' Greene said.
The first came in the first inning, when Twins rookie Miguel Sano hit a two-run home run. The second came in the fourth inning, when Danny Santana hit a two-run triple.
At that point, the Tigers trailed by five.
"When you're down that quickly in a game," Ausmus said, "It's tough to come all the way back."
In the fourth, Eddie Rosario led off with a triple. Then Aaron Hicks singled and Eric Fryer reached on a bunt single before Santana's triple.
All-Star Brian Dozer drove him in on a sacrifice fly.
"There was a couple times I couldn't put guys away and a couple times i fell behind early and they were in hitters counts and put good swings on the ball," Greene said.
He was pulled after allowing a solo home run to Trevor Plouffe in the fifth inning.
Greene threw 4 2/3 innings, allowing seven runs -- all earned -- on seven hits. He struck out three and walked two.
Unlike Saturday's contest, when Alfredo Simon was shelled, the Tigers offense didn't prove to be any kind of comeback threat against right-hander Kyle Gibson.
Gibson allowed one run on four hits over seven innings. He tamed the Tigers once and for all after walking two batters to open the seventh inning, when he induced a groundball double play from Nick Castellanos.
Ian Kinsler had three hits.
With the loss, the Tigers enter the All-Star break at .500. They trail the Royals by a season-high nine games in the American League Central.
"I think it's a good break and at the right time," Martinez said. "So we're just going to go on the break and take some rest and recharge the batteries and finish the season strong."

tigers game in box 0713

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
At Target Field, Minneapolis

What happened: The Tigers lost to the Twins, 7-1. ... They dropped the final three games of a four-game set and sit at .500 entering the All-Star break and a season-high nine games behind the Royals in the American League Central. ... Shane Greene was socked, allowing seven earned runs on seven hits over 4 2/3 innings. ... Twins right-hander Kyle Gibson was stellar, allowing one run over seven innings.

Starting off: Greene put the Tigers in an early hole, allowing a two-run home run to Twins rookie Miguel Sano in the first inning. He allowed four runs on four hits in the fourth inning. Greene, who had spent the better part of last month at Triple-A Toledo, walked three and struck out two. "Pretty similar," manager Brad Ausmus said. "Still some balls that were getting hit over the zone."
At the plate: Ian Kinsler had three hits. ... Marc Krauss drove in a run on a groundout in the second inning. ... Victor Martinez doubled in the ninth inning.
On the mound: Tigers relievers combined to throw 3 1/3 innings of scoreless relief on two hits. ... Ian Krol, Al Alburquerque, Bruce Rondon and Blaine Hardy each struck out a batter.

Streak snapped: Yoenis Cespedes went 0-for-3, snapping his 15-game hitting streak at Target Field, which was tied with former Indians first baseman Travis Hafner for most in the stadium's history. ... Cespedes left the game in the seventh inning with a sickness, Ausmus said.
Overheard: "Hopefully this break comes at a good time for us," Ausmus said.
Three stars: 1. Gibson, 2. Danny Santana (2-for-3, 2 RBIs), 3. Sano
Up next: Friday vs. Orioles.
tigers notes 0714

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- The American Leaguers are playing 'Follow the leader' at the All-Star Game.
And the leader -- to nobody's surprise -- is Tigers left-handed ace David Price.
Price's influence in this year's festivities extends far and wide, well past his two teammates that sat to the right of him inside a ballroom at the Cincinnati Westin during media day on Monday.
"This is hands down the most amount of friends or people I've known at the All-Star Game," Price said.
And many of them, like current teammates Jose Iglesias and J.D. Martinez and former teammates Chris Archer and Wade Davis and fellow Vanderbilt pitcher Sonny Gray, will walk around under Price's wing this year.
"He's definitely helped me a lot," Martinez said. "He's guided me the whole time I've been here."
Price, who is participating in his fifth All-Star Game, said he relishes the role of being the elder statesman for his Tigers teammates and Archer, the Rays right-handed starter who he calls "my little brother" and Gray, the Athletics right-handed starter, who texted him as soon as he landed in the city on Sunday night.
"It's awesome," Gray said. "We had dinner last night and we were together all morning so it's been great."
The strong bond between Price and Archer developed during their time with the Rays and has gotten even stronger since.
"He's like a little brother to be honest," Price said. "I see a lot of myself in him and that's why i grew so close to Arch whenever we became teammates. 
"His passion for wanting to be the best, everything about him just really reminded me of myself. He respects the game and that's the most important thing. This game rewards hard work and it has with him and i'm very happy to see that. He's like a little bro."
Like Archer, Price texts Gray before and after every start.
Said Archer: "I've been his little sidekick all day today, just kind of learning the ropes and it's really cool. I can't really explain it but he's been very critical, even before he knew who i was, he's been very critical in my development as a human and a pitcher. I'm loving every minute I can spend with him."
Said Gray: "You just know he's watching and it's really nice to have someone you know is on the sidelines.
The two work out together at Vanderbilt in the off-season.
"I was in that position a couple years ago," Price said about his first All-Star Game appearance. "I know how overwhelming this can be and how much stuff they're going to ask us to do and the biggest piece of advice I can give any young guy is you have to have fun. Whatever it is that you need to do to have fun and enjoy yourself at the All-Star Game, that's what you need to do. This is for the fans but it's about us. We earned our right to be here."
And Price has earned the right to be the ringleader of the AL newcomers.
"Having all of these guys together -- especially J.D. and Iglesias -- it's very special to be a part of that," he said. 
"It gives me more stuff to do. Those are some of my best friends so just to have those guys with me as well is awesome."
tigers main 0714

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- They are excited to be at the All-Star Game.
It's crazy, Tigers leftfielder J.D. Martinez said. He hasn't been to the field yet, shortstop Jose Iglesias said, "But that's definitely going to be a beautiful experience."
Both Martinez and Iglesias were present and accounted for on Monday at All-Star media day and both were joined by their families.
But there is one integral person missing to both of their first All-Star experiences: Miguel Cabrera.
"Big," Martinez said. "I would have loved for to be here with him just to be able to follow him around and follow his lead and let him show me the ropes."
Cabrera is Martinez's baseball playing idol and has helped the leftfielder mold into the All-Star form that he is today.
He was selected as the American League starter at first base but was unable to play because of a Grade 2 left calf strain suffered on July 3.
The injury will keep him out of action for at least six weeks.
Many of the other All-Stars spoke about Cabrera's absence, with fellow Venezuelans Felix Hernandez and Salvador Perez both showing their support for the Tigers' first baseman.
Said Hernandez, the Mariners right-hander: "I miss him. He's so fun."
Said Perez, the Royals catcher who regularly converses in chit chat with Cabrera inside the batter's box: "I really wanted him to be here."
But perhaps nobody is missing Cabrera more this weekend than Iglesias, who has grown close to the superstar slugger and serves as his little brother of sorts.
"I"m very disappointed," Iglesias said. "It would have been a lot different but unfortunately he's hurt. It would have been huge for him to be here with me for my first All-Star Game. I would have liked to share that with him.
"He's a guy that I'm always with him, I talk to him about everything so he's a big part of me being here today."
Cabrera, 32, is a 10-time All-Star in 13 big league seasons. In 2015, he is hitting .350 with 15 home runs and 54 RBIs.
Both Martinez and Iglesias said they talked to Cabrera via text on Monday but the young shortstop said he worried about making him wish that he was here.
"I texted him and sent him pictures and stuff but I don't want to bother him too much because I know how much he would like to be here," Iglesias said.
Cabrera has been an All-Star in six consecutive seasons.
With his absence, Angels first baseman Albert Pujols will start at first base and hit third for the AL in the All-Star Game on Tuesday night.
"I'm really happy to have Pujols on my team," Iglesias said. "He's a legend, a guy that's been around a long time."
Said Tigers left-handed ace David Price: "Everybody in here wants to see Miguel. He's awesome. His act on the field, which fans get to see quite a bit, is the most unique I've ever seen of a player of that caliber. For a player of his caliber to be as good as he is with as much fun as he does, it's crazy."
tigers six 0714

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- David Price is open to a contract extension with the Tigers.
But as of Monday, when he spoke at All-Star media day, the two sides haven't made any progression on the lucrative, long-term offer that the left-hander will receive.
"No, not yet," he said. "I was open to it."
When asked if that meant the Tigers had not contacted his camp, Price said, "You'll have to ask my agent."
Price said he did not believe he would be traded by the July 31 non-waiver trade deadline and said, "This is hands down one of the most talented teams I've ever been on."
"I don't think it will happen, I don't. We have a very very talented team. ... So we just need everybody to do their part, come to the field, work hard and have fun."
The Tigers are at .500 on the season and stand nine games back of the Royals in the American League Central. They are 
"If we can get back to the baseball playing we did the first two weeks of the season, the sky's the limit," he said. "We need to play by those capabilities and I think everybody in our clubhouse understands that."
The Tigers are 15-3 in Price's starts this year. He is scheduled to hit free agency in the off-season and will likely command a contract not unlike the $215 million one that right-hander Max Scherzer signed with the Nationals last winter.
Price is 9-2 with a 2.38 ERA this season. He has 115 strikeouts in 125 innings.
tigers six 0715

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- There are the differences.
Max Scherzer plays for the Nationals. He pitches in the National League. He  faces one fewer hitter most times through the lineup.
But the similarities between the Nationals, whom he signed a seven-year, $215 million deal in the off-season, and the Tigers, whom he spent the previous years pitching for, are there.
"A lot of similarities," he said. "They're both really good organizations and I can only say great things about the Detroit Tigers organization. 
"A lot of things the Washington Nationals do remind me of the standard held in Detroit. Both have great clubhouses and characters in both ends."
There is also another difference the Nationals' ace points out: "I'm better in 2015 than I was in 2014."
And the numbers make no bones about it. In his first year with the Nationals, Scherzer has a 2.11 ERA and 0.78 WHIP. He has 150 strikeouts in 132 innings and a no-hitter to his name.
He capped one of the most impressive two-start runs in major league history with a no-hitter against the Pirates on June 20. In that start, he lost a perfect game bid after hitting a batter with two outs in the ninth inning. In the start before, he shut out the Brewers on one hit -- a bloop single in the seventh inning.
"I'm attacking the zone at a higher rate, throwing a lot more first-pitch strikes but I also feel like the guys in the National League are a lot more aggressive."
Scherzer has pitched deeper into games this year and when asked about it, said it was a "chicken and egg question." 
"The number of times I feel like I've had guys swing at the first pitch of the game is way more than I've ever had in the AL. I'm throwing more strikes and guys are swinging more so I think they're both kind of playing into each other. That's the reason I'm being more efficient and pitching deeper into games."
Scherzer said he still keeps in touch with some of his former Tigers teammates and exchanges text messages from time to time with manager Brad Ausmus.
"I saw (David) Price, talked to him a little bit," he said. "His whole fiasco of making fun of Torii was pretty funny."
And while there are a number of similarities between the Nationals and Tigers, the big difference is that Scherzer, one of the game's best starting pitchers, isn't helping the Tigers win ballgames this year, which he did at a frequent rate over the past few years.
"My transition to Washington has been enjoyable," he said.
tigers main 0715

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- Jose Iglesias knows he's an All-Star.
You can see it in the way he walks and talks and in his flawless fielding in the field and brash batting stance in the batter's box and in the confidence he exudes inside the clubhouse.
But he didn't think he would be an All-Star this early, not a year removed from missing the entire 2013 season with stress fractures in each leg.
"I didn't expect this one so quickly," he said. "But I'm blessed for it."
Iglesias, the Tigers' young shortstop, was rubbed shoulders with the best baseball players in the world the past two days in Cincinnati. He is the best fielding shortstop in the American League and arguably all of baseball, with only Atlanta's Andrelton Simmons in his company. 
"Iglesias is a pretty good shortstop," former Tiger Jhonny Peralta said. "I mean he's one of the best defenders I see. Quick guy, he can do everything and he deserves to be here."
And this season, much to the surprise of many, Iglesias is hitting at an All-Star pace as well. For the season, he has a .314 batting average and .364 on-base percentage with impressive walk-to-strikeout ratios at the bottom of the Tigers' lineup.
"Those type of numbers I'm not expecting to hit, especially after missing a full year," Iglesias said. "But I'm healthy and when a player at this level is healthy, they're capable of doing good things."
After easing him into an everyday role in spring training, there have been a couple bumps in the road -- he has missed time with groin soreness and a bruised shin -- but has played in 77 of the team's 88 games so far and is the biggest reason for their improved defense.
But it's not his fielding or his hitting that has him smiling so much nowadays, it's his health -- most specifically the shins that sidelined him -- and ability to be in the lineup on a consistent basis.
"I think when the doctor cleared me and he said the fractures are gone and your bones are fine and we saw the pictures and there was no fractures there, it got me confident enough to let me play every single day," he said inside the American League clubhouse before Tuesday's All-Star Game. "Obviously we took it easy in spring training you know we wanted to be for sure, we wanted to be concerned about that. But at this point, I'm really happy that I turned the page with that."
This season, Iglesias said, he has adjusted his diet to include more green vegetables -- broccoli is his favorite -- in order to improve his chances to stay healthy.
"You gotta eat some more green vegetable stuff you gotta get some shots of calcium, try to get a lot of Vitamin D so those little things help you get better so i did a lot of that in the off-season."
He wasn't a fan of vegetables, he said, but, "I think i am now so that's a good thing. so i think every time you improve your diet you improve your physical condition.
"I think like everything in baseball, the quicker you make an adjustment, the better you're going to be in the future so i think to myself, 'Why waste time and start doing it now?' and keep my weight and keep my shape and keep my range the longest I can. I love this game so i would like to play as long as I can."
His first All-Star experience has been about meeting the other players and learning from them, most notably Angels first baseman and future Hall of Famer Albert Pujols, who he spent 20 minutes talking with.
"It's a great experience," Iglesias said. "Talking about everything on and off the field so i think those are the little things that make you as a person and a human being better. There's a reason why you came here to talk to those guys that have been around a long time."
It's the same day-to-day dialogue he gets from Tigers veterans like Miguel Cabrera and Victor Martinez and Ian Kinsler.
"I'm glad we have it in Detroit as well, but I think it's special to talk to people from other organizations and perspectives so i'm really happy about that."
That happiness is understandable. This time last year, he was watching the All-Star Game -- and the entire Tigers' season -- from his couch in Florida. This season, he is making highlight reel play-after-play, doing his job at the bottom of the order -- "Putting the ball in play," he said -- and will get the opportunity to open eyes in front of the baseball world in the Midsummer Classic. 
Asked whether he likes hitting or fielding, Iglesias thought long and hard before opting for the glove and said it depends on what helps the team most at the moment.
"It depends," he said. "Sometimes you make a nice play for the team to save a couple runs. It's huge. Sometimes you get the big hit and that's huge, too, so it just depends what the situation of the game dictates but overall, I'll go with fielding. It's more fun."
And while his newfound appreciation of vegetables is only one small reason for this year's success, and while he can't keep up with his mini-me sidekick throughout the All-Star festivities, son Jose Jr., who sported a Cincinnati Reds mustache courtesy of a Sharpie marker during the game's red carpet parade on Tuesday afternoon -- "He can eat whatever," Iglesias laughed -- it's just another reason for his many smiles.
"I like broccoli," Iglesias said. "I like broccoli a lot. Straight up, with mashed potatoes and steak."
He whistled.
"Bueno."

By Anthony Fenech

CINCINNATI -- He was nervous.
He is nervous before every game, whether it's spring training or regular season or postseason or, in this case, the All-Star Game.
"Absolutely," David Price said. "If you're not nervous then I don't think you care enough. And if you care as much as I care about baseball and trying to be as good as possible, you have to be a little nervous about it."
The Tigers' left-handed ace worked out of a familiar but unfamiliar role for the American League in Tuesday night's All-Star Game at Great American Ballpark in Cincinnati: As a reliever.
Price debuted as a reliever with the Rays in 2008 -- he has always been a starter but worked out of the bullpen in the stretch run that season -- and said he would draw on that experience as much as he could in the Midsummer Classic.
"Go out there and get three outs," he said.
And he did, allowing XXX runs on XXX hits in the third inning. He struck out XXXXX.
"I'm going to handle it like a start," Price said before the game. "I gotta keep my routine the same. If I don't keep my routine the same, I'm not going to feel the same out there and I don't want to go out there and feel not as ready and have my body as ready."
His pregame routine, though, wasn't the same. Coming out of the bullpen, Price was unable to do his stretches in centerfield or long toss in rightfield.
"The biggest thing is playing catch in rightfield," he said, noting that he could only stretch out to about 80 feet in the bullpen.
Price said he feels like a reliever's job is tougher than a starter's in some respects, because the bullpen men don't know when they will pitch in any given game. 
"It's definitely different from starting," he said. "As a reliever, you have to have a routine just like a starter does. I think being a reliever is tougher than being a starter. As a starter, you know what day you're throwing and you know what time the game starts but as a reliever, you might have your number called in the second pitch of the game -- you never know what can happen out there -- I think being a reliever is probably tougher in that sense."
Price said he wouldn't change anything about his arsenal in the short stint and wouldn't necessarily ramp up his velocity.
"I try and throw every pitch as hard as i can so if it's there, it will be, if not, i'm not going to try to throw it any harder," he said. 
When he was a youngster pitching in relief he said, there was no routine: "I just went out there and threw."
Price pitched in his fifth All-Star Game -- his first came in St. Louis in 2009 -- and said every one is special, but this one more so because of the amount of friends he has on the team.
Inside the AL clubhouse at Great American Ballpark, his locker neighbors were Rays starting pitcher Chris Archer and Tigers rightfielder J.D. Martinez.
"You'll always remember the guys in this locker room," Price said. "It allows you to have more relationships in baseball and that's what this is all about."
all-star gamer 0715

By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press

CINCINNATI -- First, you have to be in the right place at the right time.
And standing on the mound in the bottom of the fourth inning at Great American Ballpark on Tuesday night, Tigers left-handed ace David Price was.
Then, he said, good things have to happen to you.
And when the American League scored two runs in the top of the fifth inning in the 86th All-Star Game, they did.
After throwing a scoreless inning, RBI hits from Rangers first baseman Prince Fielder and Royals outfielder Lorenzo Cain made Price the winning pitcher in the Midsummer Classic as the AL beat the National League, 6-3.
"I was just in there at the right time," Price said. "I'll take it."
Price steamrolled through the NL murderer's row of Nationals leftfielder Bryce Harper, Diamondbacks first baseman Paul Goldschmidt and Giants catcher Buster Posey -- striking out the first two swinging -- and was the second consecutive Tiger to win the All-Star Game. Last year in Minnesota, right-hander Max Scherzer was the winning pitcher.
"To get three outs and be the guy that gets the decision in a game like this is always neat," Price said. 
He retired the side on a line drive to rightfield off the bat of Posey and threw 11 pitches.
With the exhibition win, the AL representative in the World Series will receive home-field advantage.
Price entered the game in a 1-1 tie and half an inning later, after the hits from Fielder -- a single -- and Cain -- a double -- was in line for the win, a position he wouldn't surrender as the AL won their third straight game.
Taking the loss was Dodgers left-hander Clayton Kershaw, who allowed two runs on three hits.
Every Tiger in uniform made an appearance.
Shortstop Jose Iglesias went 0-for-2 and rightfielder J.D. Martinez went 0-for-1.
"It was fun, it was really fun," Martinez said. "You always get that energy when you go out there, that nervousness feeling. It kind of felt like one of those, this is my first days in the big league moment. It kind of felt like where you're just nervous and anxious and you want to go out there and do something to help the team."
In the seventh inning, he grounded out to shortstop on the first pitch from Brewers reliever Francisco Rodriguez.
In Iglesias' two at-bats, he struck out swinging against Mets right-hander Jacob DeGrom and grounded out to third base against Pirates reliever Mark Melancon.
"I was excited," Iglesias said. "It was my first at-bat in my first All-Star Game. It was just another at-bat but this one was different."
In the bottom half of the eighth inning, Iglesias made one of his patented pristine defensive plays, ranging far in the hole to backhand a hard grounder from Dodgers catcher Yasmani Grandal. 
Throwing across his body, Iglesias outed him with ease.
Said Price: "I'm used to it."
Said Martinez: "Oh, whatever. Another play."
Angels centerfielder Mike Trout led off the game with a home run to rightfield off NL starter Zack Greinke. For the second consecutive year, Trout took home All-Star Game MVP honors, going 1-for-3 with a walk and two runs scored, including the game-winner on Cain's double in the fifth inning.
Fielder drove in two runs. Pirates centerfielder Andrew McCutchen hit a solo home run in the seventh inning and Twins Brian Dozier -- who downed the Tigers on a three-run, walk-off home run on Friday -- hit a solo home run in the eighth inning.
"I enjoyed it as much as I can," Iglesias said. "I had a really good time and I'm blessed to be here. Bottom line we got the 'W.'"
Price and Scherzer's consecutive victories mark the first time an AL team has had back-to-back All-Star Game winners since the Yankees in 1947-48.
After two days off, the second half of the baseball season begins on Friday, when the Tigers will host the Orioles to open a seven-game homestand at Comerica Park.
"Win baseball games," Price said.
On Tuesday, he was in the right spot in the right time. On Friday, it's the right spot in the right time for the Tigers to follow his orders.
